title: Word frequency counter
prompt: Write a Python function `word_freq(text)` that returns a dict mapping each lowercase word in `text` to how many times it appears. Ignore punctuation (commas, periods, exclamation marks and so on), but KEEP an apostrophe that is inside a word: don't is ONE word and its key in the dict is "don't" (not "dont"). Apostrophes used as quotation marks around a word, as in 'hello', are not part of the word.

title: Password strength check
prompt: Write a Python function `is_strong(password)` that returns True only if the password has at least 8 characters, at least one digit, at least one uppercase letter, and at least one special character (a character that is not a letter or a digit). Otherwise it returns False.

title: Binary search (in memory)
prompt: Write a Python function `binary_search(items, target)` that takes a list of integers sorted in ascending order with no duplicates and returns the index of `target`, or -1 if it is not in the list. Use an iterative binary search that halves the search range at each step. Do not use the bisect module or list.index().

title: Word frequency (approach hint)
prompt: Write a Python function `word_freq(text)` that returns a dict mapping each lowercase word in `text` to how many times it appears. Ignore punctuation (commas, periods, exclamation marks and so on), but KEEP an apostrophe that is inside a word: don't is ONE word and its key in the dict is "don't" (not "dont"). Apostrophes used as quotation marks around a word, as in 'hello', are not part of the word. Approach: do NOT strip punctuation with re.sub. Instead lowercase the text and use re.findall to pull out the words directly, where a word is a run of word characters that may contain apostrophes between word characters. Then count the words.

title: Record pack/unpack (24-byte format)
prompt:
Write two Python functions for a fixed-width binary record of exactly 24 bytes: an 8-byte unsigned integer key stored big-endian, followed by a 16-byte ASCII payload padded on the right with NUL bytes.
`pack_record(key, payload)` takes an int key and a str payload and returns the 24 bytes. It raises ValueError if the key is not in the range 0 to 2**64-1, if the payload is longer than 16 characters, or if the payload contains a non-ASCII character or a NUL character.
`unpack_record(data)` takes 24 bytes and returns a tuple (key, payload), where payload is a str with the NUL padding removed. It raises ValueError if data is not exactly 24 bytes.
Approach: use the struct module with one fixed format string.

title: Record pack/unpack (struct format hint)
prompt:
Write two Python functions for a fixed-width binary record of exactly 24 bytes: an 8-byte unsigned integer key stored big-endian, followed by a 16-byte ASCII payload padded on the right with NUL bytes.
`pack_record(key, payload)` takes an int key and a str payload and returns the 24 bytes. It raises ValueError if the key is not in the range 0 to 2**64-1, if the payload is longer than 16 characters, or if the payload contains a non-ASCII character or a NUL character.
`unpack_record(data)` takes 24 bytes and returns a tuple (key, payload), where payload is a str with the NUL padding removed. It raises ValueError if data is not exactly 24 bytes.
Approach: use the struct module with the format string '>Q16s' (a big-endian unsigned 64-bit integer followed by 16 bytes). A '16s' field takes a bytes object and pads it with NUL bytes by itself, so pass payload.encode('ascii'). To unpack, use the same format string, remove the padding with rstrip(b'\x00') and decode with 'ascii'. Check the arguments first and raise ValueError; payloads of 0 to 16 characters are all valid.

title: Search a sorted record file (Python)
prompt:
Write a Python function `search_file(path, key)`. The file at `path` holds fixed-width binary records, 24 bytes each, sorted by key in ascending order with no duplicate keys. The first 8 bytes of each record are the key as a big-endian unsigned integer; the remaining 16 bytes are the payload, which you can ignore. `search_file` returns the index of the record whose key equals `key` (the first record has index 0), or -1 if there is none. An empty file has no records.
The file can be much larger than memory, so never read all of it. Approach: open the file in binary mode; compute the number of records with os.path.getsize(path) // 24; do an iterative binary search over the record indices; to read the key of record i, call f.seek(i * 24), then f.read(8), then int.from_bytes(data, 'big'). Do not use the mmap module.

title: Search a record file (structural hint)
prompt:
Write a Python function `search_file(path, key)`. The file at `path` holds fixed-width binary records, 24 bytes each, sorted by key in ascending order with no duplicate keys. The first 8 bytes of each record are the key as a big-endian unsigned integer; the remaining 16 bytes are the payload, which you can ignore. `search_file` returns the index of the record whose key equals `key` (the first record has index 0), or -1 if there is none. An empty file has no records.
The file can be much larger than memory, so never read all of it. Approach: open the file in binary mode; compute the number of records with os.path.getsize(path) // 24; do an iterative binary search over the record indices; to read the key of record i, call f.seek(i * 24), then f.read(8), then int.from_bytes(data, 'big'). Structure: start the code with `import os`. Open the file exactly once, before the loop, using `with open(path, 'rb') as f:`, and put the whole binary search loop and all return statements inside that with block.
